title: Batching
explain: Batching merges many independent work items into one more efficient downstream operation. It pays off whenever a call has a fixed cost, such as a round trip, headers, an fsync or a commit, that a bigger payload spreads out. The price is latency and more complicated failure handling, so I always say how the batch is formed and what bounds the wait.
model:
**Where does the batch come from?**

1. **There is already a staging area** (a queue, a table of pending rows): take N items from it and send them together.
2. **There is no staging area** (a client producing events): buffer in memory and flush at **N items or K ms, whichever comes first**.

```
item -> [ buffer ] --(N items or K ms)--> one downstream call --> per-item results
```

**Why it works:** an operation costs `fixed + per_item * n`. The fixed part is paid once per batch, not once per item. On the client this mainly cuts per-message overhead (Kafka producer `batch.size` and `linger.ms`, bulk inserts).

**What you pay for:** waiting latency (up to K), partial failure (return per-item results, retry only the failures, keep processing [idempotent](#/sd/f/idempotency)), size caps by count and bytes, loss of an unflushed buffer on a crash, and ordering rules within and across batches.

details.q: Show me the benefit with numbers. A call costs 5 ms fixed plus 0.1 ms per item; send 1,000 items one call at a time.
details.a: One item per call: 1,000 x 5.1 = 5,100 ms. Batches of 100: 10 x (5 + 10) = 150 ms. The saving comes from paying the 5 ms overhead 10 times instead of 1,000. Bigger batches give diminishing returns because the per-item part never shrinks.

details.q: Why must a client-side buffer have a time trigger, not only a size trigger?
details.a: At low traffic a size-only trigger starves: with 2 events per second and N = 100, an event can wait about 50 s. 'N items or K ms' bounds the added latency to K regardless of load.

details.q: Events arrive at 400/s; the batcher flushes at 50 events or 100 ms since the first buffered event. What does a typical batch look like?
details.a: Filling 50 takes 50 / 400 = 125 ms, longer than the 100 ms linger, so the timer fires first: about 400 x 0.1 = 40 events. At higher rates the size cap wins instead. Tuning is deciding which trigger you want to be the usual one.

details.q: A bulk write of 100 items returns success for 97 and an error for 3. What does the caller do?
details.a: Read per-item results, retry only the 3 (or park the permanently invalid ones in a dead-letter place), and acknowledge the 97 individually. Retrying the whole batch duplicates the successes unless writes are idempotent; dropping the batch loses them. One bad item must not poison 99 good ones.

details.q: Someone wants a 500 ms linger on card authorisation to save calls to the processor. Your p99 target is 200 ms.
details.a: No. The linger is added to every request, so the budget is blown before the call starts. Batch background and throughput-oriented work; on an interactive path use a tiny linger that fits the budget or no batching at all.

details.q: What happens to the buffer if the process crashes?
details.a: An in-memory buffer is lost. If items matter, buffer durably (write-ahead file, local queue) or accept the loss window of up to K ms and N items. This is the same trade-off as an `fsync` interval.

details.q: What can go wrong with ordering?
details.a: Items in a batch may be applied in an order the caller did not intend, and a retried batch can overtake a later one. Define the order (per key, per batch, none) up front, and keep one in-flight batch per key if order matters.

details.q: Where else does batching show up in a design?
details.a: It tames hot-key writes (aggregate locally before touching the counter, see [time bucket counter](#/sd/f/time-bucket-counter)), makes [fanout](#/sd/f/fanout) to many downstreams affordable, and cuts per-request overhead in logging, metrics and DB inserts.

prompts.q: Explain batching and when it is worth it.
points: Merge many items into one downstream operation
Pays when there is a fixed cost per call
A numeric example (overhead 5 ms, per-item 0.1 ms)
Costs: latency, partial failure, loss on crash
In-memory buffer flushed at N items or K ms, whichever first
Swap the buffer out so new events keep accumulating during the call
Per-item results; retry only failures; idempotent processing
Size caps by count and bytes

prompts.q: When would you refuse to batch, or keep the linger tiny?
points: Linger adds directly to every request
Batch background or throughput work instead
Items that cannot be lost need a durable buffer
